newsitem.title: GUAM: Recovery work at Guam plane crash site halted.
newsitem.headline: Recovery work at Guam plane crash site halted.

text.p: The grim work of recovering more than 150 bodies from the wreckage of a Korean Air Lines jumbo jet was halted on Thursday so that U.S. experts could examine the site, military authorities said.
In a briefing near the hilltop crash site on this Pacific island, U.S. Air Force Colonel Al Riggle said the recovery efforts would probably not resume until the afternoon.
"There could be about 100 more bodies in the fuselage. But the military is waiting for the National Transportation Safety Board personnel to arrive on the scene, who then will take over from us."
He said crash experts had arrived from the United States mainland and were now resting.
He said the wreckage, strewn across a wide stretch of mainly scrub brush and razor-sharp tropical grasses, had finally stopped smouldering.
But with temperatures hovering around 35 Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) conditions remained difficult for the 300 military personnel at the scene.
Military officials gave up hope on Wednesday evening of finding any more survivors amid the wreckage.
Officials said 29 people had survived, 72 were confirmed dead and 153 remained missing.
The Boeing 747 slammed into a hillside as it approached the airport during a torrential downpour in the early hours of Wednesday.
Flight 801 from Seoul was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crew, including dozens of vacationers and several South Korean politicians.
At Guam's airport a few kilometres (miles) away, hysterical mourners mixed with holidaymakers as hundreds of Koreans arrived to claim the bodies of loved ones.
The 250 South Koreans who reached the island 24 hours after the crash included wailing old women in black mourning garb, stone-faced KAL officials and a group of Seoul nurses flown in to help.
"What will I do now? How will I live on?" shrieked an elderly Korean woman, who nearly collapsed in the airport arrival lounge.
The airline had set up a hospitality and information centre for the bereaved and promised regular briefings. But many family members of victims demanded more and better information.
"The airline seems to be passing the buck at a time when families need them the most," said Roger Kang, a vacationing Seoul businessman who was helping families of victims.
"Many of them still have not seen a proper list of who has survived and who is dead."
James Lee, an official of the 10,000-member Guam Korean Residents Association, said Koreans tended to mistrust KAL "for its past record of accidents".
Aviation experts said the cause of the crash was likely to be known soon. Attention has focused on the bad weather and the lack of a guidance system that was being repaired.

The flight data and voice recorders arrived in Washington on Wednesday night and work on deciphering the information began immediately, according to a spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board.
An airline representative at Guam said the pilot of ill-fated Flight 801 should have had ample information to land the aircraft even without the guidance system, known as a glide slope.
"The glide slope has been out of service for more than four weeks for repair, and KAL has been flying in nightly for four weeks," he said, asking not to be identified.

Marty Salfen, senior vice president of the International Airline Passengers Association, said KAL had an accident rate of 1.91 per million departures over the past 10 years against the worldwide rate of 0.581 per million.
The figure does not include the loss of KAL flight 007, a Boeing 747 that strayed into Soviet airspace in 1983 and was shot down. All 269 people aboard died.
Guam, a U.S. territory, is home to a large U.S. military presence and has become an increasingly popular resort destination among Asians.
Some residents said the KAL flight was popular among locals because it connected with flights leaving Seoul and was the cheapest way to fly from the Pacific island to the U.S. mainland.
